Flow SQL writes notify live views the way auto-CRUD does (live table events only: they fire no hooks.yaml entry and no event flow, see below). Every `run: sql` / `run: sql_dynamic` statement that INSERTs (incl. REPLACE / INSERT OR …), UPDATEs or DELETEs a schema table - a leading `WITH …` included, at any nesting depth (if / for_each / parallel / on_error) - is recorded, and when the run's writes are durable the framework broadcasts one `{table, action}` event per table and action, to SSE and WebSocket subscribers alike.

Durable means: after COMMIT for `transaction: true` (a rollback or failed commit emits nothing); for a non-transactional flow each statement commits on its own, so its event is sent even if a later step fails. on_error handlers run outside the transaction, so their writes count as durable.
Never announced: `_benmore_*` framework tables, `sqlite_*`, full-text index tables, temp/attached-schema tables, and a single-statement write that changed zero rows.

Flow writes do not fire hooks.yaml or `on: event` flows. Those run only for auto-CRUD writes (create, update, delete, restore, batch and /api/_transaction; not NDJSON /ingest or bulk import), workflow transitions, POST /api/_groups/create and approved MCP command applies. A `run: sql` / `sql_dynamic` write - in a request, cron, async or data-event flow, or an on_error handler - sends its table event (above) but runs no hook entry (`notify:`, `email:`, `webhook:`, `sql:`) and starts no event flow; neither does a cron.yaml `sql:` job or a hook's own `sql:`. Do that work in the flow: `run: notify` (notify_step), `run: email`, `run: webhook`, or more steps.

Scope: the flow's signed-in session (auth: required flows) scopes the event exactly like an auto-CRUD write by that user. A run without one (cron, webhook, data-event and async jobs, public flows) takes its audience from trusted trigger data only: the `_group_id` / `user_id` an async job keeps from the signed-in caller who queued it, or a data event's row (its tenant key column or user_id), never request input. With a tenant, a write to a tenant-keyed table reaches that tenant (and admins); without one, only admins. A cron job (any run with no session and no request input) has no trigger tenant, so write the statement to RETURN the tenant column - `UPDATE bookings SET stale = 1 WHERE ... RETURNING studio_id` - and the event reaches each tenant the written rows name (at most 256 per table and action per run) plus admins; without it the write still reaches admins only, and members' live views stay stale until they refetch. A write to an owner-keyed (user_id) table reaches its owner in full and every other reader as the generic `{action:'refresh'}` with no table name. Publicly readable tables stay unscoped. Either way each subscriber is re-checked per event (live session, table read access, token scopes) and receives only `{table, action}` - never row values.
